If the SAS process fails to start, verify: The saspath is correct and points to a valid SAS executable You have execute permissions on the SAS executable SAS is properly licensed on your local machine
Check that your SAS options are valid Review the SAS log for error messages Ensure your WORK directory has sufficient space Verify that AutoExec files (if specified) are accessible and valid

Add New Connection Profile SAS 9.4 (remote - SSH) Connection Profile Managing Connection Profiles The stdio connection type was contributed upstream by Andreas Menrath in sassoftware/vscode-sas-extension#1771.

A SAS Viya connection profile includes the following parameters: "connectionType": "rest" Name Description Additional Notes endpoint URL for the SAS Viya server. An example is https://example.sas.com. Appears when hovering over the status bar. context Context for Compute Server Please see SAS Documentation for more information. clientId Registered Client ID for SAS Viya Please contact your SAS administrator. authorization_code and refresh_token grant types are required. Leave blank for Viya4 2022.11 and later. clientSecret Registered Client Secret for SAS Viya Please contact your SAS administrator. Leave blank for Viya4 2022.11 and later. Depending on your SAS Viya version, the values for the prompts differ slightly. For SAS Viya 2022.11 and later, you can leave Client ID and Client Secret prompts empty and simply press Enter. (The built-in Client ID vscode will be used.) For SAS Viya 2022.10 and before (including SAS Viya 3.5), you need to provide a Client ID and secret. For more information about Client IDs and the authentication process, please see the blog post Authentication to SAS Viya: a couple of approaches. A SAS administrator can follow the Steps 1 and 2 in the post to register a new client.

When running in Posit Workbench with a SAS Viya OAuth integration configured by your administrator, the extension can use the SAS Viya token that Posit Workbench already manages for you, so you do not sign in to SAS Viya a second time. Your administrator sets this up as a custom OAuth integration in Posit Workbench, and you sign in to it once from the Posit Workbench homepage (Managed Credentials). Two optional profile settings control this: Name Description Additional Notes authentication How to sign in to SAS Viya: "auto", "workbench", or "sasLogon". Defaults to "auto". workbenchIntegration GUID of the Posit Workbench OAuth integration to use. Only needed when several integrations point at the same SAS Viya server. Ask your administrator for it. "auto": in Posit Workbench, use the OAuth integration whose token URL is the SASLogon/oauth/token URL of endpoint (or the integration set in workbenchIntegration). If you have not signed in to that integration yet, a message asks you to sign in to it in Posit Workbench, with the option to sign in with SAS Logon instead. Outside Posit Workbench, or when no integration matches, the extension signs in with SAS Logon as before. "workbench": always use the Posit Workbench OAuth integration. If none is available, connecting fails with an error that explains why. "sasLogon": always sign in with SAS Logon in the browser. With a Posit Workbench token, the extension keeps the token in memory only and gets a fresh one from Posit Workbench before it expires. Signing out from the Accounts menu stops the extension from using the token until you sign in again; it does not sign you out of the integration in Posit Workbench. { "connectionType": "rest", "endpoint": "https://example.sas.com", "authentication": "auto" }

In Viya environments, SAS Administrators have the option to specify the allowDownload property on the context definition for the SAS Compute Server. This property determines the appearance of the Download menu item in these areas: Tables in the Libraries pane. Files and folders in the SAS Content and SAS Server panes. The Results pane. The following screenshot provides an example context definition setup:

You can customize when the SAS log is displayed in the bottom panel by using the following extension settings. These settings apply to all connection profiles: Name Description Additional Notes SAS.log.showOnExecutionStart Show SAS log on start of execution default: true SAS.log.showOnExecutionFinish Show SAS log on end of execution default: true To access the SAS settings, select File > Preferences > Settings. Search for "sas" and then click SAS in the search results to view the SAS extension settings. You can edit the settings directly in the settings.json file by clicking Edit in settings.json. Example settings.json { "SAS.log.showOnExecutionFinish": true, "SAS.log.showOnExecutionStart": false, "SAS.connectionProfiles": { "activeProfile": "viyaServer", "profiles": { "viya4": { "endpoint": "https://example-endpoint.com", "connectionType": "rest", "sasOptions": ["NONEWS", "ECHOAUTO"], "autoExec": [ { "type": "line", "line": "ods graphics / imagemap;" }, { "type": "file", "filePath": "/my/local/autoexec.sas" } ] } } } } tip To view the SAS log as a text file, click the ... icon on the top right of the OUTPUT panel, and select Open Output in Editor.

The SAS extension includes many features to help you access your data, write and run code, and create SAS notebooks. You can use the SAS extension to access your libraries and tables. If you are connected to a SAS Viya server, you can also access SAS Content. You can edit code using many of the same features that are available in the SAS code editor. You can run SAS code and create a custom task to run a specific SAS file. You can create an interactive SAS notebook. In Positron, SAS also gets its own console, the Viewer, Plots, and Connections panes, the Data Explorer, and Posit Assistant. See Positron SAS Extension Features.

After you configure the SAS extension for a SAS Viya environment, you can access SAS Content. To access SAS Content: Click the SAS icon in the VS Code activity bar. Click Sign In. Your SAS Content should be displayed after you sign in. You can create, edit, delete, upload, download, and run files stored on a SAS server. note SAS Content requires a profile with a connection to a SAS Viya server.
You can drag and drop files and folders between the SAS Content pane and File Explorer. You can drag and drop a file from SAS Content into your SAS code. SAS generates a FILENAME statement for you.

After you configure the SAS extension for a SAS Viya, SAS 9.4 (local), or SAS 9.4 (remote-IOM) environment, you can access your connected libraries. You can use the Libraries pane to delete a table, drag and drop tables into your SAS program code, view table data, or view table properties.

When viewing table data, you have the following options available for each column (accessible by hovering over a column and clicking the menu button): Column pinning: Each column can be pinned to the left or the right of the data viewer to have an always on-screen view of important columns. Sort: Each column can be sorted ascending or descending. To add multiple columns to a sort, click the menu for each column and select the sort type. Sort priority will be displayed next to each column's direction icon. Properties: Clicking properties will reveal the properties for the specific column chosen. Filtering results: Results can be filtered by specifying where conditions in the filter bar and pressing enter. To reset the filter, click the clear (X) button.
Table Properties can be revealed using the "Properties" menu item in the libraries pane or by clicking "Properties" from a table's column menu.

After you configure the SAS extension for a SAS Viya environment, you can access SAS Server. To access SAS Server: Click the SAS icon in the VS Code activity bar. Click Sign In. Your SAS Server files should be displayed after you sign in. You can create, edit, delete, upload, download, and run files stored on a SAS server. note SAS Server requires a profile with one of the following connection types: SAS Viya, SAS 9.4 (remote - IOM), SAS 9.4 (local)
You can drag and drop files and folders between the SAS Server pane and File Explorer.

SAS Clinical Acceleration stores clinical study files in a controlled repository on a SAS Viya server. The Positron SAS extension adds views to their own Clinical Acceleration sidebar, next to the SAS one in the activity bar, so that you can browse the repository, work on files in your own workspace, check them back in, and run clinical jobs. The Clinical Acceleration icon appears in the activity bar, and the views with it, when the active SAS profile is a SAS Viya profile, you are signed in, and the server runs the Clinical Repository service. The extension finds the service on its own and uses your SAS Viya sign-in, so there is nothing to configure.

Clinical Repository: the shared store. Files open read-only. Clinical Workspace: your own area on the server. Files open for editing, and saving a file saves it to your workspace. Clinical Jobs: your clinical job runs and what each run used and wrote. Clinical Job Schedules: your schedules that run clinical jobs at set times. Clinical Jobs and Clinical Job Schedules appear when the server also runs SAS Clinical Job Management. Clinical Repository Properties (collapsed at first): the details of the item you select in the Clinical Repository view. Clinical Version History (collapsed at first): the versions of the file you select in the Clinical Repository view. To refresh the Clinical Repository view and detect the service again, click Refresh in the title bar of the view.

Expand folders in the Clinical Repository view and click a file to open it read-only. Studies and organizations appear as top-level items. Administrators manage organizations, so you cannot rename or delete them. Right-click an item to see the actions you can use. The extension shows an action that changes an item only where you have write permission. New Folder: create a folder in the selected folder. Rename: rename a file or folder. Delete: move the selected items to the recycle bin of the Clinical Repository. You can restore them with the Manage Data Repository application of SAS Clinical Acceleration. You cannot delete studies or organizations. Upload and Upload and Expand: add files to a folder. Upload and Expand unpacks a zip file into the folder. Download: save the selected items to your computer. A folder or a selection of several items arrives as a zip file. Copy Path: copy the repository path of the selected items. An upload asks for an optional comment and an optional version. Leave the version empty to upload without versioning, which works without any special privilege. Enter a version such as 1.0 to create a versioned file. You can also enter MAJOR or MINOR to raise the version of a file that is already versioned.
Your workspace is a private area on the server. Files in the repository stay unchanged until you check in your changes from the workspace.

Right-click an item in the Clinical Repository view and use one of these actions: Check out to Workspace > With Content: reserve the file for yourself and copy its content to the workspace. Check out to Workspace > Without Content: reserve the file without copying its content to the workspace. Copy to Workspace > Copy Latest Version: copy the current version of a file without reserving it. On a folder, the action is Copy Folder and copies the files in it. Copy to Workspace > Copy Folder Structure: copy the folders, with their subfolders, but not the files. To copy an older version, right-click it in the Clinical Version History view and select Copy to Workspace. A checked-out file has a CO badge in both the Clinical Repository and Clinical Workspace views. The badge is highlighted for your own check-outs and dimmed for check-outs by other users. Point to the badge to see who has the file.

Click a file in the Clinical Workspace view to edit it. Save the file as usual to send the changes to your workspace. Right-click a file or folder for these actions: New File and New Folder: create an item in the selected folder. Without a selection, the item goes to the top level of the workspace. Rename: rename an item. The extension closes the open editors of the item, and reopens a renamed file. Delete: remove the selected items from your workspace. This does not change the repository. Upload, Upload and Expand, and Download: move files between your computer and the workspace. Copy Path: copy the workspace path of the selected items.

When your changes are ready, right-click a file or folder in the Clinical Workspace view and select Check In. For a folder, the extension checks in every eligible file in it. The extension asks only the questions that apply to your files: For files that are new to the repository, whether to enable versioning, and the first version. For files that you checked out without versioning, the same two questions. For files that are already versioned, whether to raise the Major or Minor version. An optional comment. Select Undo Check out to give up your changes to a checked-out file. Only the person who checked out a file can check it in or undo the check-out. A copy from Copy to Workspace cannot replace a file that is already in the repository, because only a check-out lets you add a version. When you try, the extension says which files it left out and why: a copy that is not checked out to you, or a file checked out by someone else. To check in a changed copy, check the file out first with Check out to Workspace > Without Content, which leaves your workspace file as it is. The SAS Clinical Repository output channel lists every file that was left out.

Select a versioned file in the Clinical Repository view and the Clinical Version History view lists its versions, newest first. Point to a version to see who created it, when, its size, and its comment. Click a version to open it read-only. Right-click a version to download it, compare it, or copy it to your workspace. To turn versioning on or off for a file, right-click it in the Clinical Repository view and select Enable Versioning or Disable Versioning. Changing versioning needs a versioning privilege on the server. The extension stops and tells you when the server reports that you have no such privilege. The Clinical Repository Properties view shows the details of the selected item. For a file, it lists the size, the lock state, the version, the check-out state, and whether the copy of the file in your workspace is in sync with the repository. For files and folders, it also lists Your permissions, the permissions the server grants you on the item, such as READ and WRITE, and Your versioning privileges. They explain a missing action: without WRITE on a file, for example, Check out to Workspace is not offered. Permissions can differ between folders, and adding new files to a folder is not the same as changing a file that is already there.

You can compare any two files or versions from the repository, your workspace, and the version history. Right-click the first file or version and select Select for Compare. Right-click the second one and select Compare with Selected. To compare two items in the same view, select both, right-click one of them, and select Compare Selected.

Open a .sas file from the Clinical Workspace or Clinical Repository view and run it as you run any SAS program. The program runs in the SAS console session of the active profile. Running a program does not write its results to your workspace, and SAS Clinical Acceleration keeps no record of the run. To keep a result file, save it on your computer and upload it. To run a program with a record of its inputs and outputs, run it as a clinical job, as described in Run a program as a clinical job. A .sas7bdat or .xpt file from the Clinical Repository or Clinical Workspace view opens in the Data Explorer. The extension copies the file into the WORK library of the SAS session first, so a SAS session must be running. See Positron SAS Extension Features for more about the Data Explorer.

A clinical job is a .cjob file that lists SAS programs to run, in order, and the parameters they take. A job in the repository can also list the repository files it reads and where its outputs are checked in. SAS Clinical Acceleration runs the job on the server and writes a manifest (a .cmnf file) next to it. The manifest is the audit record of the run: which programs ran and how they ended, the parameter values, and every file the run read and wrote, with its version. To run a job: Right-click a .cjob file in the Clinical Workspace or Clinical Repository view and select Run Clinical Job. With a .cjob file open in the editor, you can also click Run Clinical Job in the editor title bar. Enter a value for each parameter of the job. The prompts start with the default values of the job. For a file or folder parameter, pick the file or folder from the view the job is in. A notification shows the state of the run. To cancel the run, click Cancel in the notification. When the run ends, a notification says how it ended, with buttons to open the log, the results, and the manifest report. A job writes its log (.log), listing (.lst), and manifest next to the job file unless the job names other locations.

To run a single .sas program from your workspace as a clinical job, right-click it in the Clinical Workspace view and select Run as Clinical Job. With the program open in the editor, you can also select Run as Clinical Job from the Run menu in the editor title bar or from the context menu of the editor. The first time, the extension creates a job with the name of the program next to it, such as adsl.cjob for adsl.sas, and runs it. Later runs reuse that job. Unsaved changes in the editor are saved first, because the job runs the file on the server. If a job of that name already exists and runs other programs, you can create a new job, such as adsl-2.cjob, or replace the existing one. The job and its log, listing and manifest are written to your workspace. To keep a record in the repository, check in the job and the program, and run the job from the Clinical Repository view.
documents.s: Run a program as a clinical job

documents.t: A .cjob file opens in the clinical job editor, a form with these sections: General: the description of the job. Programs: the programs the job runs, in order. Click Add Program... to pick a program, use the arrows to change the order, and click Open to open a program. Leave Version empty to run the latest version of a program. Parameters: the values asked for when the job runs. The programs see them as macro variables, so a name must be a valid SAS name. Each parameter has a type (text, masked text, number, date, file, or folder) and an optional default. Output locations: the folders for the log, the results, and the manifest. ./ is the folder of the job. Repository runs: the repository files and folders the job reads, and how its outputs are checked in. These settings apply only when the job runs from the Clinical Repository view. Paths of programs and output locations are stored relative to the job, as SAS Clinical Acceleration stores them. The editor checks the job as you edit it and lists problems, such as a job without programs or an invalid parameter name, above the form. Save the job as you save any file. Undo and redo work as in a text editor. Click Run to save and run the job, or Open as JSON to edit the file as text. To create a job, right-click a folder in the Clinical Workspace view, select New Clinical Job..., and enter a name. The job opens in the editor. Jobs in the Clinical Repository view open read-only. To change one, copy it or check it out to your workspace.

The Clinical Jobs view lists your runs, newest first, with their state. Runs that have not ended update on their own while the view is visible. Click Load more... at the end of the list for older runs. Expand a run to see its manifest: Programs: each program with its result (such as successful, warnings, or errors) and run time. Parameters: the values the run used. Inputs and Outputs: the files the run read and wrote. Hover over a file to see its path, version, size and checksum (MD5, repository files only). Logs and Results: the log and listing of the run. Check-in failures: outputs of a repository job that were not checked in. Click a file to open it. A versioned repository file opens at the version the run used. Right-click a run for more actions: Show Manifest Report and Export Manifest...: show or save the manifest report, described in the next section. Open Log and Open Results: open the log or the results of the run. Open Job: open the job file. Run Again: run the job again with the same parameter values, without prompts. Cancel Run: cancel a run that has not ended. Copy Run ID: copy the ID of the run, for example for an administrator. Remove from List: hide the run in Positron. You can select several runs and remove them together. To hide every finished run, click Clear Finished Runs in the title bar of the view. Runs that are still going stay in the list. Hidden runs are hidden only in Positron, for your user on that server: the run history on the server, with its manifests, stays as it is. To see hidden runs again, click Show Hidden Runs in the title bar; they are marked as hidden, and Restore to List brings one back. Restore All Hidden Runs is in the ... menu of the view. note A run of a repository job checks its outputs in to the repository. If an output file is checked out, or you lack write permission for its folder, the run ends with a check-in error, and Check-in failures lists the files. The outputs of a workspace job stay in your workspace.

A schedule runs a job at set times, with set parameter values, under your user. To create one: Right-click a .cjob file in the Clinical Workspace or Clinical Repository view and select New Schedule.... You can also click Schedule... in the clinical job editor, or New Schedule (the plus sign) in the title bar of the Clinical Job Schedules view and pick the job. Enter a name for the schedule. Select when the job runs, and answer the questions for that choice: Once or On several dates: the dates and the time of day. Every few minutes or Hourly: the interval, and for hourly runs the minute of the hour. Daily or Weekly: the interval in days or weeks, the days of the week for weekly runs, and the time of day. Monthly or Yearly: the month for yearly runs, either a day of the month (such as the 15th) or a weekday (such as the first Monday), and the time of day. Monthly runs also take an interval in months. For repeated runs, enter the first day and when the schedule ends: never, on a date, or after a number of runs. Confirm the time zone. It defaults to the time zone of your computer. Enter the parameter values of the job. A notification shows the next run. The Clinical Job Schedules view lists your schedules with when they run. Expand a schedule to see its job, its parameter values, and its next runs, as the server calculates them. Right-click a schedule for more actions: Run Now: run the job now with the parameter values of the schedule. The run appears in the Clinical Jobs view. Edit Schedule...: change the name, the times, the time zone, or the parameter values. The questions start with the current values. Disable Schedule and Enable Schedule: stop and resume the runs without deleting the schedule. Delete Schedule...: delete the schedule. The job itself is kept. Copy Schedule ID: copy the ID of the schedule. A schedule whose job was deleted, or that you can no longer read, is marked with a warning. The view lists the schedules that run as you. To see the schedules of all users that the server shows you, click Show All Users' Schedules in the title bar. Other users' schedules are marked with their owner, and you can only copy their ID. Click Show My Schedules to go back.

The manifest report shows the manifest of a run as one page, for review or for a quality check. It lists the job, how the run ended, who ran it and when, the parameter values, the programs with their results and run times, and each input and output file with its version, size, modification time, and MD5 checksum. For a repository job, it also shows how outputs are checked in and which outputs failed to check in. To show the report, do one of the following: Click Show Manifest Report on a run in the Clinical Jobs view. Click Show Manifest in the notification at the end of a run. Right-click a .cmnf file in the Clinical Workspace or Clinical Repository view and select Show Manifest Report. In Positron, the report opens in the Viewer, where Posit Assistant can read it. Click a path in the report to open that file. A versioned repository file opens at the version the run used. Ask the Assistant, for example, which version of a dataset a run read. To save the report, select Export Manifest... in the same places. Save it as an .html file for the report, or as a .json file for the manifest as the server returns it. The paths in an exported report are not links. note The server returns the manifest of a run only while its .cmnf file is unchanged. The next run of the same job overwrites that file, so the report of the earlier run is no longer available. Export the report of a run to keep it.

The extension reads your permissions from the server and shows only the actions you can use. If it cannot read them, it shows all actions and the server decides. note A server can still refuse an action, such as a check-out without write permission or a versioning change without the privilege. This is the server enforcing its rules. The SAS Clinical Repository output channel lists the message from the server. Clinical Repository Properties shows your permissions on the selected item. Ask a SAS Clinical Acceleration administrator for the missing permission.

The views use the active SAS Viya profile. Switch profiles to work with another server. The views do not detect changes made by other users or other applications. Click Refresh to see them. You cannot search the repository, restore deleted items, or change permissions. Use SAS Clinical Acceleration for those tasks.

The Problems panel contains error and warning messages that are generated by the SAS log when you run a program. Errors and warnings in the Problems panel are not cleared until you rerun the code. The Quick Fix option enables you to remove items from the Problems panel without rerunning the code. To use the Quick Fix options: Open the Quick Fix menu in one of these ways: Click a message in the Problems panel and then click the corresponding Show Code Actions icon in the code editor. Click the Show fixes button for the appropriate message in the Problems panel. Select one of the following options: Ignore: current position - clears the currently selected problem from the Problems panel and the code editor. Ignore: warnings - clears all warnings from the Problems panel and the code editor. Ignore: error - clears all errors from the Problems panel and the code editor. Ignore: all - clears all problems from the Problems panel and the code editor. tip You can use the Problems panel as a to-do list when you are debugging your code. When you correct an error in your code, open the Quick Fix options for that error and select Ignore: current position to remove the error message from the list.

The Positron SAS extension adds SAS to Positron as a language with its own console. SAS code runs in that console, and its results go to the usual Positron panes: the Viewer, the Plots pane, the Data Explorer, and the Connections pane. Posit Assistant can see the results and explore SAS data. The extension works with SAS Viya, with SAS 9.4 or SAS Analytics Pro over SSH, and with a local SAS installation. Some features depend on the connection type. See Features by Connection Type for details. Builds on the SAS Extension for Visual Studio Code The SAS Extension for Positron extends the SAS Extension for Visual Studio Code, so the rest of this documentation still applies in Positron. Connection profiles, code editing features such as syntax highlighting, completion, snippets, and folding, SAS Content, SAS Server, libraries, and SAS notebooks work as described there. This page covers what Positron adds or changes. To run SAS in Posit Workbench, see SAS with Posit Workbench.

Each entry in the SAS.connectionProfiles setting becomes a runtime named SAS (profile) in the Positron interpreter picker. Configuring the SAS Extension describes how to create profiles. In Positron, the commands described in Running SAS Code and Fixing Errors and Warnings send code to the SAS console, and results open in the Viewer pane instead of a Result tab. Start a console: pick a SAS runtime in the interpreter picker. When a .sas file becomes the active editor and no SAS console runs, Positron starts the preferred SAS runtime. Run code from the editor: Run All SAS Code, Run Selected or All SAS Code, and Run Region send the code to the SAS console, as Positron does for R and Python. Run code in the console: type SAS code at the sas> prompt. A statement is complete when it ends with a semicolon. Read the log: the console shows the full SAS log of your code: the source, notes, warnings, and errors. Lines from the code that the extension wraps around yours are hidden. The same lines go to the SAS Log output channel. Find problems: for code run from a .sas file, errors and warnings from the log appear as squiggles in the editor and in the Problems pane. The SAS.problems.log.enabled setting turns this off. Code typed into the console or generated by Posit Assistant reports problems in the console only. See a summary: a run with errors ends with a SAS Error message that lists the error lines. A run with only warnings ends with a warning count. Interrupt: the console interrupt button cancels the running code on SAS Viya. Over SSH and stdio, SAS cannot cancel a submission: the console stays busy until the code finishes, and a message offers Restart Session, which stops SAS. Each console connects with the profile of the runtime you picked, and each console has its own SAS session. You can run several SAS consoles side by side, for example local SAS and SAS Viya, and shutting one down does not affect the others. The Data Explorer, the SAS data file viewers, and Posit Assistant work with the console in the foreground.

In Posit Workbench, a SAS Viya profile signs in with the token of a Workbench OAuth integration for SAS Viya, so users sign in to SAS Viya once, on the Workbench homepage. Without a matching integration, or outside Workbench, the extension signs in with SAS Logon in the browser. The profile settings authentication and workbenchIntegration control this. See Remote SAS Viya.

The extension wraps each submission in SAS Output Delivery System (ODS) HTML5 output, with graphs drawn as inline PNG images. Viewer: each run's HTML report opens in the Viewer pane as a file named sas-output-<n>.html. In Positron builds that cannot open HTML files in the Viewer, the report opens in a SAS Output panel. Plots pane: each graph also goes to the Plots pane. The Plots pane opens after the report, so a run with graphs ends with the plot in front. Text copy for Posit Assistant: each run's result also carries a plain-text copy of the report, with titles and tables. The console shows only a short note that names the panes with the output. If your code opens its own ODS HTML or HTML5 destination, the extension does not add its own ODS statements.
documents.s: Results in the Viewer and Plots Pane

documents.t: SAS datasets and views open in the Positron Data Explorer. Open one from the Connections pane, the Data Connections pane, or a .sas7bdat or .xpt file. The Data Explorer runs its queries as SAS code in the console session. The following screenshot shows SASHELP.CLASS, opened from the Data Connections pane of a SAS Viya console. Right-click a table and choose Open in Data Explorer. The summary panel on the left lists the columns with a histogram and the share of missing values for each. The grid on the right shows the rows. The Data Connections pane next to the Data Explorer for SASHELP.CLASS. The summary panel lists the five columns, and the grid shows the rows. Sorting: sort by one or more columns. Row filters: compare (=, !=, <, <=, >, >=), between, not between, is missing, is not missing, is empty, is not empty, is true, is false, set membership, and text search. Text search supports contains, does not contain, starts with, ends with, and regular expression match, with or without case sensitivity. Column profiles: missing-value counts, summary statistics, histograms for numeric columns, and frequency tables. Dates: numeric columns with a SAS date format (for example DATE9. or YYMMDD10.) are date columns. Columns with DATETIME or DATEAMPM formats are datetime columns. Positron offers date-range filters for both. Convert to Code: creates a PROC SQL query that selects the dataset with the current filters and sort order. Expand a column in the summary panel to see its profile. This one shows the Height column of SASHELP.CLASS, with its histogram, the number of missing values, and summary statistics. The Data Explorer with the Height column expanded in the summary panel. It shows a histogram and the missing count, minimum, median, mean, maximum, and standard deviation. Sort and filter from the column menu or the filter bar. The next screenshot sorts Height in descending order and keeps the rows where Height > 60. The status line shows that 12 of the 19 rows remain. The Data Explorer with Height sorted in descending order and the filter Height greater than 60. The status line shows 12 rows of 19. Convert to Code turns the current filters and sort order into code. The dialog offers the syntax to use, and here it shows the PROC SQL query for the view above. Copy Code copies it to the clipboard. The Convert to Code dialog with the code syntax sas, showing a PROC SQL query that selects from SASHELP.CLASS where Height is greater than 60, ordered by Height descending. The Data Explorer refreshes its row counts after each console run.

The extension lists the libraries of the running SAS session in Positron. Which pane it uses depends on the Positron version. Connections pane: in Positron 2026.09 and earlier, or when the Positron setting dataConnections.enabled is off, a SAS (profile) connection appears in the Connections pane. It shows libraries, their tables and views, and the columns with their types. Select the preview icon of a table to open it in the Data Explorer. The tree refreshes after each console run. Data Connections pane: in Positron 2026.10 and later with the Positron setting dataConnections.enabled turned on, the Data Connections pane lists a SAS (profile) connection for each running SAS console. It shows the same library tree, and preview opens a table in the Data Explorer. Positron reads dataConnections.enabled at startup, so restart Positron after you change it. SAS Server Files: on SAS Viya, a read-only SAS Server Files (profile) connection browses the file system of the compute session. The fileNavigationRoot and fileNavigationCustomRootPath profile settings set its root folder. In the Data Connections pane, text files up to 512 KB show their content in the details view. In the Connections pane, previewing a file opens it in an editor. The Libraries view that Accessing Libraries and Tables describes is hidden in Positron, because the Connections and Data Connections panes replace it. On SAS Viya, the SAS Content and SAS Server views stay in the SAS sidebar, as described in Accessing SAS Content and Accessing SAS Server. The SAS sidebar on SAS Viya with the SAS Content view expanded. It lists the folders Jobs and Flows, Model Repositories, Products, Public, and Users. The SAS sidebar on SAS Viya with the SAS Server view expanded to the Home folder of the compute session.

The extension opens .sas7bdat and .xpt files in the Data Explorer. Open the file from the Explorer, or from a view such as the Clinical Repository. Datasets: for a .sas7bdat file on disk, the extension assigns a library to the file's folder with a LIBNAME statement. Transport files: for an .xpt file, the extension detects the format from the file header: XPORT version 5, XPORT version 8 or 9, or PROC CPORT. It unpacks the file into a library in the WORK folder of the session. Several datasets: when a transport file holds more than one dataset, a picker asks which ones to open. Files from other views: files that are not on disk, such as files from the Clinical Repository or SAS Content views, are copied into the WORK folder first. This copy also works when SAS runs in lockdown mode. The file class.sas7bdat opened in the Data Explorer through a SAS (viya) console. The extension assigned the library _FVIEW to the file's folder. The dataset picker for a transport file with two datasets, CLASS and FISH. warning SAS data files open through the SAS session, so a SAS console must run first. For files on disk, SAS reads the path itself, so the SAS server must be able to see the same path.

The extension gives Posit Assistant access to the SAS session and its results. Language model tools: sas_list_libraries lists the libraries of the session. sas_list_tables lists the datasets and views in a library. sas_describe_table returns the columns, types, lengths, formats, and row count of a dataset. sas_export_saspy_config returns the active profile as a saspy configuration, for SAS code chunks in Quarto documents with the sasquatch R package. Posit Assistant uses the commands below instead. Commands for Quarto reports: SAS: Export saspy Configuration writes the active profile as sascfg_personal.py, next to the open .qmd file or in the workspace folder. It never asks before replacing a different file: it keeps the old one as sascfg_personal.py.old-<timestamp> next to it and tells you where. For a SAS Viya profile, the file uses saspy's HTTP access method and looks for the access token each time saspy connects: the SAS_VIYA_TOKEN environment variable, a variable on the Python main module, the Workbench OAuth integration (with posit-sdk and the integration ID), and then the token file. The file never contains secrets. See SAS Viya with OAuth Tokens. SAS: Save Viya Token for saspy writes the access token of the extension's SAS Viya sign-in, including a Posit Workbench token, to ~/.positron-sas/viya-token.json. Only you can read the file. Run it again when the token has expired. Workspace context: while a SAS console runs, the assistant knows the active profile and how to use the tools above. Results: the assistant reads the text copy of each result and looks at graphs in the Plots pane. sas-results skill: in Positron 2026.10 and later, a skill tells the assistant where SAS output goes and how to read the report in the Viewer. The first time the assistant uses the skill, Positron asks whether it may load it. Choose Allow. sas-quarto-report skill: a skill for turning a SAS analysis into a Quarto report. See Reports with Posit Assistant. Positron asks whether the assistant may load it, as for the sas-results skill. Posit Assistant asking whether it can use the sas-results skill. The conversation shows the question and the getPlot and skill steps, with Allow and Decline buttons. As an example, ask about a result. After a console run that produced a plot, the assistant looks at the plot in the Plots pane and describes it. In this answer, it describes the direction, shape, and spread of the points, notes that it read the values by eye, and suggests PROC CORR and PROC REG to measure the relationship. Posit Assistant describing a scatter plot of weight against height from a SAS run. The answer lists the direction, shape, spread, extremes, and outliers, and suggests a follow-up with PROC CORR and PROC REG.

Ask Posit Assistant for a report after a SAS analysis, for example with the /report command, and it writes a Quarto document that keeps the analysis in SAS. It does not ask whether to use R with haven or Python with pandas. The document has {sas} code chunks that run through the sasquatch R package. Before it proposes an outline, the assistant checks the setup: sasquatch: if the package is not installed, the assistant asks whether to install it. saspy: if the Python package is missing, the assistant offers to run sasquatch::install_saspy(). Connection file: the assistant runs SAS: Export saspy Configuration, unless sascfg_personal.py already exists next to the document. For a SAS Viya profile, the assistant also runs SAS: Save Viya Token for saspy before each render when the SAS_VIYA_TOKEN environment variable is not set, so the render uses your existing sign-in. A SAS report follows these rules: Setup chunk first: the first code chunk is an {r} chunk labeled setup, with library(sasquatch) and sas_connect(). With only {sas} chunks, Quarto looks for a SAS Jupyter kernel and fails. Chunk options: in a {sas} chunk, options are written *| label: load-data;. The #| form that {r} chunks use stops the render. Leave one blank line between the last *| line and the first SAS statement: without it, only the first option is read. Own SAS session: the render opens its own SAS session through saspy, not your console session. Tables in WORK and macro variables from the console do not exist there. The report loads its data from permanent libraries or files, or repeats the DATA steps. Formats: {sas} chunks produce HTML and PDF output only. Before the assistant says a report is done, it checks the {sas} chunks against these rules and renders the document. If it could not render, it says "Written, not rendered" and gives the reason. The skill is part of the extension and works in Positron 2026.10 and later. In older versions, ask for the same steps by hand.

The extension records who ran which SAS code, including code that Posit Assistant runs. Audit log: set SAS.audit.logFile to a file path to record every console submission as JSON Lines. A leading ~ expands to the home folder. Leave the setting empty to turn auditing off. An input record holds ts, executionId, code, osUser, host, positronSessionId, profile, connectionType, and, when known, sasUser, workbenchServerUrl, and workbenchSessionId. A complete record holds ts, positronSessionId, executionId, status (ok or error), errorCount, warningCount, and durationMs. Submission comment: the first line of each submission carries a comment that SAS writes to its log. The console hides it. /* positron: user=<user> session=<session> exec=<execution> */ Macro variables: each session sets &POSIT_USER, &POSIT_SESSION, and &POSIT_WORKBENCH_SESSION, so programs and autoexec files can reference them. &POSIT_WORKBENCH_SESSION is empty outside Posit Workbench. SAS Viya tags: compute sessions are named Positron SAS (<user>) and carry the user, host, and session IDs as attributes. Each console job is named positron-console, and its description holds the user, session, and execution IDs. An example audit.jsonl with one submission: {"event":"input","ts":"2026-11-02T10:15:00.000Z","osUser":"jdoe","host":"pwb-1","positronSessionId":"1a2b3c4d","profile":"local","connectionType":"stdio","executionId":"e7f8","code":"proc means data=sashelp.class; run;"} {"event":"complete","ts":"2026-11-02T10:15:01.200Z","positronSessionId":"1a2b3c4d","executionId":"e7f8","status":"ok","errorCount":0,"warningCount":0,"durationMs":1200}

On SAS Viya servers with SAS Clinical Acceleration, the Clinical Acceleration sidebar, next to the SAS one in the activity bar, shows the Clinical Repository, Clinical Workspace, Clinical Repository Properties, and Clinical Version History views. They let you browse the repository, edit files in your workspace, check files out and in, manage versions, and compare files and versions. The extension detects the service of the active profile's server and uses the existing SAS Viya sign-in. See SAS Clinical Acceleration for details.

The stdio connection type runs a SAS installation on the same machine as Positron, without SSH or SAS servers. The extension starts SAS as a child process in line mode (-nodms) and keeps it running for the session. To set up a profile, run SAS: Add New Connection Profile, select SAS 9.4 (local - stdio), and enter the path of the SAS executable. The stdio connection profile lists all settings. { "SAS.connectionProfiles": { "activeProfile": "local", "profiles": { "local": { "connectionType": "stdio", "saspath": "/opt/sas/viya/home/SASFoundation/sas" } } } } When the extension finds SAS on the machine, it adds a local profile like the one above. It looks in the paths of the SAS.localSasPaths setting, then at /opt/sas/viya/home/SASFoundation/sas (SAS Analytics Pro), then in common SAS 9.4 locations, where it uses the UTF-8 launcher bin/sas_u8, and finally for sas on the PATH. See SAS Installed with Workbench. It adds the profile once: a deleted profile stays deleted, and an existing stdio profile prevents it. The profile becomes the active profile only if no profile is active. The profile's autoExec lines run once, right after SAS starts.

Feature SAS Viya (rest) SAS 9.4 or SAS Analytics Pro over SSH (ssh) Local SAS (stdio) SAS console and editor runs Yes Yes Yes Log in the console and SAS Log channel Yes Yes Yes Editor squiggles and Problems pane Yes Yes Yes Interrupt running code Yes No, restart to stop No, restart to stop HTML report in the Viewer Yes Yes Yes Graphs in the Plots pane Yes Yes Yes Libraries in the Connections or Data Connections pane Yes Yes Yes SAS Server Files connection Yes No No Data Explorer Yes Yes Yes .sas7bdat and .xpt files on disk If the server sees the path If the server sees the path Yes .sas7bdat and .xpt files from other views Yes No No Posit Assistant tools, context, and skill Yes Yes Yes Audit log, submission comment, and macro variables Yes Yes Yes Compute session and job tags Yes No No Sign-in through a Workbench OAuth integration Yes No No SAS Content and SAS Server views Yes No No Clinical Acceleration views With SAS Clinical Acceleration No No Automatic local profile No No Yes, for SAS Analytics Pro and SAS 9.4

Interrupt over SSH and stdio: these connection types cannot cancel running code. To stop it, restart the session. Several SAS Viya servers: consoles that connect to different SAS Viya servers at the same time are not supported. Sidebar views: the SAS Content and SAS Server views and SAS notebooks use a separate session of the active profile, not a console's session. With stdio, that starts one more SAS process. No reconnect: SAS sessions do not survive a reload of the Positron window. Positron discards them, and you start a new console. Data Explorer: exporting a selection, searching the column list, and column filters are not supported. Plots: SAS draws each graph once, so the Plots pane cannot redraw it at a new size. Viewer for Posit Assistant: the assistant can read the report in the Viewer only in Positron 2026.10 and later.

After you configure the SAS extension for your SAS environment, you can run your SAS program and view the log and results. The steps to connect to SAS and run your program are different for SAS Viya and SAS 9.

To run a SAS program with a SAS Viya connection: Click the icon in the upper right corner of your SAS program window. For a secure connection to SAS Viya, you must connect with an authorization code: 2.1. If VS Code prompts you to sign in using SAS, click 'Allow'. 2.2. If VS Code prompts you to open an external website, click 'Open'. A new browser window opens so that you can log on to SAS. 2.3. Log on with your SAS credentials. 2.4. SAS returns an authorization code. Copy this code. 2.5. Paste the authorization code in the authorization box at the top of the VS Code application. VS Code connects to SAS and runs the code. The results are displayed in the application. The SAS output log and error information are displayed in the application. info Your sign in status will persist in VS Code. You can view it and sign out from VS Code's Accounts menu.
Click the icon in the upper right corner of your SAS program window. VS Code connects to SAS and runs the code. The results, log, and error status are displayed in the application.

To run a selection of SAS code: The Run Selected or All SAS Code command (F3) will automatically run selected code when you have selected lines of code in a program. If you have not selected any lines of code, SAS runs the entire program. If you have selected multiple sections of code, the Run Selected or All SAS Code command combines the code from the selections in the order in which they were selected, and then submits the combined code. The Run All SAS Code command (F8) always runs the entire program. Notes: A new session must be created the first time you run SAS code. Connection time will vary depending on the server connection. Currently, only HTML output is supported. By default, the ODS HTML5 statement is added to the submitted code. Clear the Enable/disable ODS HTML5 output option in the Settings editor for the SAS extension to disable this output. When you click Run, the code in the active tab in the editor is submitted. Make sure that the correct tab is active when you run your program. To reset your connection to SAS, run the Close Current Session command in VS Code or click the Close Session button from the tooltip of the active profile status bar item.

Open the command palette (F1, or Ctrl+Shift+P on Windows or Linux, or Shift+CMD+P on OSX) and execute the Tasks: Run Task command. Select the sas task category and then select the sas: Run sas file task. This task automatically runs selected code or all code in active editor (depending on whether you have selected any code).
documents.s: Run selected code or all code in active editor

documents.t: Open the command palette (F1, or Ctrl+Shift+P on Windows or Linux, or Shift+CMD+P on OSX) and execute the Tasks: Configure Task command. Select sas: Run sas file task. The tasks.json file opens with an initial task definition: { "version": "2.0.0", "tasks": [ { "type": "sas", "task": "Run sas file", "problemMatcher": [], "label": "sas: Run sas file" } ] } Add the file field and assign a SAS file name to it. Update the label field. Here is an example of the final task definition: { "version": "2.0.0", "tasks": [ { "type": "sas", "task": "Run sas file", "file": "my.sas", "problemMatcher": [], "label": "run my.sas code" } ] } Save tasks.json. This custom task can be run by Run Tasks... in the global Terminal menu Note: If you do not specify a file property or you assign an empty string to the file property in your task definition, the custom task will use the default properties of a built-in task.
documents.s: Custom task to run specified SAS file in workspace

documents.t: Open the command palette (F1, or Ctrl+Shift+P on Windows or Linux, or Shift+CMD+P on OSX) and execute the Tasks: Configure Task command. Select sas: Run sas file task. Add preamble and/or postamble properties and enter the SAS code. if a file is specified, the preamble and postamble will be added in the code from this file when this task is executed. If file is absent, then preamble and postamble will be added in the selected code (if you have selected code) or all code in active editor when this task is executed. { "version": "2.0.0", "tasks": [ { "type": "sas", "task": "Run sas file", "file": "code.sas", "preamble": "some code*", "postamble": "some code*", "problemMatcher": [], "label": "Run additional code" } ] }
documents.s: Custom task to run sas code with preamble and postamble added

documents.t: If you need to run a task frequently, you can define a keyboard shortcut for the task. For example, to assign Ctrl+H to the run additional code task from above, add the following to your keybindings.json file: { "key": "ctrl+h", "command": "workbench.action.tasks.runTask", "args": "Run additional code" }

The SAS extension highlights these syntax elements in your program, just as they would appear in a SAS editor: Global statements SAS procedures SAS procedure statements Data step definition Data step statements SAS data sets Macro definition Macro statements Functions CALL routines Formats and informats Macro variables SAS colors Style elements and style attributes Comment Various constants Options, enumerated option values, sub-options and sub-option values for various procedure definitions and statements

You can choose among three SAS-related color themes that control the color of the application and syntax elements. The SAS Light, SAS Dark and SAS High Contrast options mirror the themes available in SAS Studio. To specify the color theme: Select File > Preferences > Color Theme and select the theme, by name. The image below demonstrates the process changing from SAS Light to SAS Dark.

The SAS extension includes automatic code completion and pop-up syntax help for SAS keywords. The autocomplete, or code completion, feature in the code editor can predict the next word that you want to enter in your SAS program. See code completion in action below. To use the autocomplete feature: Start typing a valid SAS keyboard. Scroll through the pop-up list of suggested keywords by using your mouse or the up and down arrow keys.

The syntax help gets you started with a hint about the syntax or a brief description of the keyword. You can get additional help by clicking the links in the syntax help window. To view the syntax help: Move the mouse pointer over a valid SAS keyword in the code. In the following example, the help panel displays syntax help for the DATA= option in the PROC PRINT statement. tip Click the links in the syntax help window to navigate to the SAS online help.

Snippets are lines of commonly used code or text that you can insert into your program. The SAS extension includes snippets for SAS functions and procedures to facilitate writing your SAS programs. To access the list of snippets for a function or procedure: Type the name of a function or procedure in your SAS program. This example shows a snippet for the PROC DS2.

Regions of code are identified in your SAS program as blocks of code that can be collapsed and expanded. You can also view an outline of your program that identifies DATA steps, procedures, macro sections, and user-defined regions of code. tip You can define a custom region by adding /*region*/ and /*endregion*/ tags to the start and end of the block of code.

To format your code, open context menu and select Format Document. tip You can define custom regions as below to exclude code from being formatted. proc format library=library; /* region format-ignore */ invalue evaluation 'O'=4 'S'=3 'E'=2 'C'=1 'N'=0; /* endregion */ run;
Signature help provides information for current parameter as you are writing function calls.

SAS Notebook is an interactive notebook file that includes markdown code, executable code snippets, and corresponding rich output cells. To create a SAS notebook, select File > New File > SAS Notebook. To change a code language, click the Select Cell Language Mode button in the lower right corner of a code cell. To toggle log or ODS output display, click the More Actions (...) button in the upper left corner of the output and select Change Presentation. You can use the File menu to save your SAS Notebook to a .sasnb file, share the notebook with others, and open the notebook in another VS Code window. note Starting with Visual Studio Code version 1.93, the language for SQL files has been renamed from 'SQL' to 'MS SQL'. As a result, the SQL cell in SAS Notebook is now labeled 'MS SQL'. The SAS Extension for Visual Studio Code does not control the label of the SQL cell in SAS Notebook. The functionality of the SQL cell has not changed, however. Valid PROC SQL code continues to work in the MS SQL cell.
To export your SAS Notebook to other formats, click the More Actions (...) button on the notebook toolbar at top, and select Export. The following formats are supported.
PYTHON, R, and SQL code cells will be wrapped with PROC PYTHON/R/SQL respectively to be executed on SAS. Markdown cells will be converted to block comments.

The exported HTML will be in Light or Dark theme depending on your VS Code theme kind. By default it doesn't include SAS log into the exported HTML file. To include log, check the SAS.notebook.export.includeLog setting.

Posit Workbench and Posit Connect support several ways to bring SAS into your data science work. They differ in how closely SAS works with R and Python: side by side as separate tools, together in one editor, or mixed in the same code. This section builds on the rest of this documentation. The Features and Configurations sections describe the SAS Extension for Visual Studio Code, which the SAS Extension for Positron extends, and they still apply in Positron: connection profiles, SAS Viya and SAS 9.4 connections, SAS Content, libraries, and notebooks. The pages here add what is specific to Positron and to Posit Workbench: running SAS in the Positron console, the Positron panes, Posit Assistant, and how to set up each way of running SAS in Workbench. Scenario What you get Where SAS runs SAS within Positron SAS in the Positron console, next to R and Python, with Positron's Viewer, Plots pane, Connections pane, and Data Explorer Locally in the session, or on a remote SAS server or SAS Viya SAS in your R and Python code SAS called from R or Python code, in Workbench sessions and in content on Posit Connect SAS Viya, a SAS server, or a local SAS installation For what each scenario needs, see Requirements by Scenario. For the shared setup underneath all of them, such as single sign-on and shared home directories with SAS Viya, see Across All Scenarios.

SAS programmers who want a modern editor: SAS within Positron runs SAS with the same console, output, and data tools as R and Python, and with Posit Assistant. Start with Positron SAS Extension Features. Teams that combine languages: SAS in your R and Python code lets an R or Python program, a Quarto document, or a Shiny app run SAS code and use its results, and publish them to Posit Connect. The scenarios combine well. For example, a team can develop SAS code in Positron and call it from a Quarto report that runs on Connect.

Where SAS runs decides which connection profile you use and which features are available. If your SAS is... Use Page On SAS Viya A SAS Viya (rest) profile, with sign-in through Workbench Remote SAS Viya On a SAS 9.4 or SAS Analytics Pro server An SSH profile Remote SAS over SSH Installed on the Workbench host or in the session image The automatic local stdio profile Local SAS: SAS Installed with Workbench The Capabilities by Connection Type table lists which features each connection type supports in VS Code. For Positron, see Features by Connection Type.

In this scenario, users mix SAS and R, or SAS and Python, in the same code. R or Python prepares the data, SAS runs the analysis, and R or Python presents the results. The code runs in Posit Workbench sessions and in content that users publish to Posit Connect. The scenario has two variants that differ in where SAS runs: SAS Viya with OAuth Tokens: the code sends SAS work to SAS Viya 4. Workbench or Connect supplies the user's SAS Viya access token, so the code contains no sign-in. Local SAS Execution: SAS is installed where the code runs, and the code starts SAS as a local process.
documents.s: Scenario 3: SAS in Your R and Python Code

documents.t: SAS from R: the sasquatch package sends R data frames to SAS, runs SAS code, and returns SAS data sets to R as data frames. SAS in Quarto documents: with sasquatch loaded, {sas} code chunks run in the same SAS session as the R chunks around them. SAS from Python: the saspy package runs SAS code and moves data between SAS data sets and pandas data frames. SAS Viya services from Python: the swat package calls SAS Cloud Analytic Services (CAS) actions, and the sasctl package calls SAS Viya web services, such as model management. Shared results: Shiny apps, Quarto documents, and R Markdown reports that call SAS run on Connect for other people.

The sol-eng/sas-demo repository shows the pattern with a clinical trial simulation. Each version follows the same three steps: R generates a synthetic study data set with studies, sites, subjects, visits, and treatment groups. SAS fits a mixed-effects model with PROC MIXED or PROC HPMIXED and writes residuals, fixed effects, and variance components to SAS data sets. R reads those data sets back and draws summary tables and diagnostic plots with ggplot2. The repository contains these versions: sas/: the whole analysis in the SAS language, to run in Positron with the SAS extension. R/demo.R: an R script that calls SAS through sasquatch. quarto/demo.qmd: a Quarto document with R chunks and {sas} chunks. shiny/app.R: a Shiny app that runs the analysis on demand and shows the residuals. The core of R/demo.R looks like this: library(sasquatch) sas_connect(cfgname = "ssh", reconnect = TRUE) # Copy the R data frame into the SAS session sas_from_r(large_study_data, "large_study_data") result <- sas_run_string(" proc hpmixed data=large_study_data method=reml; class unique_subject_id study_id treatment_group visit; model outcome = visit treatment_group visit*treatment_group / solution; random intercept / subject=unique_subject_id; output out=mixed_results predicted=Pred residual=Resid; ods output ParameterEstimates=fixed_effects; run; ", capture = "both") # Return SAS data sets to R as data frames mixed_results_df <- sas_to_r("mixed_results") fixed_effects_df <- sas_to_r("fixed_effects") sas_disconnect() The demo connects to SAS Analytics Pro over SSH. The same code works with SAS Viya or with local SAS. Only the saspy configuration named in cfgname changes.

Library Language What it does How it reaches SAS sasquatch R Runs SAS code, moves data frames, and adds {sas} chunks to Quarto Through saspy and reticulate saspy Python Runs SAS code and moves pandas data frames STDIO, STDIO over SSH, or HTTP to SAS Viya swat Python and R Calls CAS actions on SAS Viya CAS HTTP or binary protocol sasctl Python Calls SAS Viya web services HTTPS to SAS Viya sasquatch does not connect to SAS itself. It calls saspy.SASsession() through reticulate, so every connection option comes from the saspy configuration.

saspy reads connection definitions from a sascfg_personal.py file. Each definition is a Python dictionary, and SAS_config_names lists the definitions you can use. These access methods matter for this scenario: Access method When to use it Required keys Standard input and output (STDIO) SAS is installed on the same Linux host or container as the code saspath STDIO over SSH SAS is installed on another Linux host saspath, ssh, and host HTTP SAS Viya 4, through the Compute service url (or ip), and usually context saspy uses STDIO when a definition has neither an ssh key nor a java key. It uses HTTP when a definition has a url or ip key. saspy looks for sascfg_personal.py in the saspy installation directory, then in the current directory, then in ~/.config/saspy/, and then in the rest of the Python path. In Python, saspy.SASsession(cfgfile=...) points to a specific file. The sasquatch function sas_connect() accepts only cfgname, so R users rely on the search order. sasquatch also provides configure_saspy(), which creates the file in the saspy installation directory. The following example shows one definition for each access method: SAS_config_names = ['local', 'ssh', 'viya'] local = {'saspath': '/opt/sas/viya/home/SASFoundation/sas'} ssh = {'saspath': '/opt/sas/viya/home/SASFoundation/sas', 'ssh': '/usr/bin/ssh', 'host': 'sas.example.com'} viya = {'url': 'https://viya.example.com', 'context': 'SAS Studio compute context'} The viya definition also needs an access token. SAS Viya with OAuth Tokens shows how Workbench and Connect supply it.

Posit Workbench Posit Connect Who runs the code The signed-in user, in their session The content process, for each viewer or on a schedule SAS Viya token Workbench User OAuth Provider (Custom OAuth integration) Connect OAuth integration, Viewer or Service Account Token function in R rstudioapi::getOAuthCredentials() connectapi::get_oauth_credentials() or connectapi::get_oauth_content_credentials() Token function in Python posit.workbench.Client().oauth.get_credentials() posit.connect.Client().oauth.get_credentials() or get_content_credentials() Local SAS SAS on the Workbench host or in the session image SAS on the Connect host or in the content image Code that works in a Workbench session needs two changes for Connect. It needs the Connect token function, and the Python environment with saspy must be published with the content. sasquatch content uses reticulate, so publish its Python environment as for any R content that uses reticulate.

Write the analysis in R or Python and keep the SAS code in strings, .sas files, or Quarto {sas} chunks. Connect to SAS with the saspy definition for your variant. See SAS Viya with OAuth Tokens or Local SAS Execution. Move data with sas_from_r() and sas_to_r() in R, or with df2sd() and sd2df() in saspy. Disconnect at the end with sas_disconnect() in R or sas.endsas() in Python. A short Python equivalent of the R example: import saspy sas = saspy.SASsession(cfgname='local') sas.df2sd(study_df, table='study') result = sas.submit(""" proc means data=study mean std; class treatment_group; var outcome; output out=summary mean=mean_outcome; run; """) summary_df = sas.sd2df('summary') sas.endsas()

sasquatch keeps one SAS session for each R process. Content on Connect that serves several viewers from one R process shares that session. A Quarto document with {sas} chunks needs an {r} chunk first that runs library(sasquatch) and sas_connect(). The {r} chunk makes Quarto use the knitr engine. Without it, Quarto uses the Jupyter engine and looks for a SAS kernel. In a {sas} chunk, chunk options start with *| and end with ;, for example *| label: load-data;, and one blank line must follow the last option line, or only the first option is read. The #| form fails, because knitr treats SAS comments like that. {sas} chunks produce HTML and PDF output only. A rendered document opens its own SAS session. It does not see tables in WORK from another session, such as a Positron console. sas_connect() passes only cfgname to saspy. Options such as an access token must come from sascfg_personal.py. SAS Viya with OAuth Tokens shows how. saspy STDIO and STDIO over SSH work only with SAS on Linux or UNIX. Data moves between the languages as copies. Large data sets take time to transfer.

In this variant, SAS is installed where the R or Python code runs. saspy starts SAS as a child process and talks to it over standard input and output (STDIO). No SAS server, network connection, or sign-in is involved. For the libraries and the overall pattern, see Scenario 3: SAS in Your R and Python Code. To send SAS work to SAS Viya instead, see SAS Viya with OAuth Tokens.

SAS next to your code: the SAS process runs on the same host or in the same container as R or Python, under the same Linux user. Direct file access: SAS reads and writes the same file system as your code, including your home directory. The same code everywhere: a Workbench session and Connect content use the same saspy definition, as long as SAS is at the same path.

Linux. saspy STDIO does not work with SAS on Windows. SAS installed in one of these places: On the Workbench host, for sessions that run there In the session image, for Workbench with Kubernetes or Slurm On the Connect host, or in the content image when Connect runs content off-host A SAS license that is valid where SAS runs saspy in the Python environment, and sasquatch for R users

Create sascfg_personal.py in the saspy installation directory or in ~/.config/saspy/. A STDIO definition needs only saspath, the path to the SAS startup command: SAS_config_names = ['local'] local = {'saspath': '/opt/sas/viya/home/SASFoundation/sas', 'options': ['-fullstimer']} /opt/sas/viya/home/SASFoundation/sas is the SAS path in SAS Analytics Pro and SAS Viya-based installations. A SAS 9.4 installation usually uses a path such as /opt/sasinside/SASHome/SASFoundation/9.4/bin/sas_u8. options takes a Python list of SAS startup options. The optional autoexec key takes a string of SAS code that saspy submits after SAS starts, for example a libname statement. R users can create the file with sasquatch and then edit it: sasquatch::install_saspy() sasquatch::configure_saspy() configure_saspy() writes sascfg_personal.py to the saspy installation directory, with an empty definition named config_name. Replace it with the local definition above.

SAS checks its license at startup, wherever it runs. Running SAS on Connect for viewers can need a different license from running it in Workbench sessions. Confirm with SAS that your license covers each place SAS runs. License SAS in the installation, or pass the license file at startup. For SAS Analytics Pro, a definition can pass the license file as a startup option: local = {'saspath': '/opt/sas/viya/home/SASFoundation/sas', 'options': ['-licensefile', '/opt/sas/license/license.jwt']}

Install SAS and its license on the Connect host, or build them into the content image. Make sure that the Linux user that runs the content can start SAS and read the license. Publish the Python environment with saspy along with the content. Place sascfg_personal.py where saspy finds it on Connect. Python content can include it in the bundle. R content can use ~/.config/saspy/ for the user that runs the content.

In R: library(sasquatch) sas_connect(cfgname = "local") sas_from_r(mtcars, "cars") sas_run_string(" proc reg data=cars; model mpg = wt hp; output out=fit predicted=pred residual=resid; run; ") fit <- sas_to_r("fit") sas_disconnect() In Python: import saspy sas = saspy.SASsession(cfgname="local") cars = sas.sasdata("cars", "sashelp") print(cars.means()) cars_df = sas.sd2df("cars", libref="sashelp") sas.endsas() The following screenshot shows this Python code in a Positron console in a Workbench session. saspy starts SAS as a child process, print(cars.means()) shows the PROC MEANS result, and cars_df appears in the Variables pane as a pandas data frame. A Positron Python console running saspy with the local definition. SAS starts, the means of the sashelp.cars data set print, and the data set is copied to a pandas data frame that shows in the Variables pane. In a Quarto document, load sasquatch and connect in a setup chunk. Later {sas} chunks run in that session: ```{r} #| include: false library(sasquatch) sas_connect(cfgname = "local") ``` ```{sas} proc print data=sashelp.class(obs=5); run; ```

saspy STDIO starts one SAS process for each session. Each process uses memory and processor time on the host or in the container. The SAS process runs as the same Linux user as the code. SAS has the same file permissions as that user, and no other identity. SAS work libraries are temporary. Save results to a permanent library or return them to R or Python before you disconnect. On Connect, a SAS process starts with the content process, not in a separate SAS server. Size the content resources for SAS.

In this variant, R and Python code sends SAS work to SAS Viya 4. Posit Workbench or Posit Connect signs the user in to SAS Logon and gives the code a SAS Viya access token. The code passes the token to saspy, swat, or sasctl and never handles a password. For the libraries and the overall pattern, see Scenario 3: SAS in Your R and Python Code.

No sign-in in code: users sign in to SAS Viya once in Workbench, and their code reads a short-lived token. The same sign-in for the Positron SAS extension: a SAS Viya console in Positron uses the same Workbench integration. See Remote SAS Viya. The user's own SAS Viya identity: SAS Compute sessions, SAS Cloud Analytic Services (CAS) sessions, and SAS Viya web service calls run with the permissions of the signed-in user. Token refresh in Workbench: Workbench refreshes the token when SAS Logon issues a refresh token. Code asks Workbench for a token each time it connects. Per-viewer access on Connect: with a Viewer integration, each viewer of a Shiny app runs SAS as themselves. Shared access on Connect: with a Service Account integration, rendered and scheduled content runs SAS with one shared identity.

SAS Viya 4 with the Compute service, reachable over HTTPS from Workbench sessions and Connect content A SAS Viya administrator who can register OAuth clients in SAS Logon saspy for SAS Compute, swat for CAS, or sasctl for SAS Viya web services For Workbench: Workbench with Custom OAuth integrations (a Preview feature in the Enhanced and Advanced tiers) HTTPS access to Workbench, and the Job Launcher with launcher-sessions-callback-address set RStudio Pro, Positron Pro, or VS Code sessions. Custom OAuth credentials do not reach JupyterLab sessions. R: the rstudioapi package. Python: the posit-sdk package, with Workbench 2026.01.0 or later. For Connect: OAuth integrations, which need the Enhanced or Advanced tier R: the connectapi package. Python: the posit-sdk package.

Register one SAS Logon client for Workbench and another for Connect. Separate clients let SAS Viya audit logs show which product made each call. A SAS Viya administrator registers each client with a POST to https://viya.example.com/SASLogon/oauth/clients. The request needs an administrator token with the clients.write scope. The following body registers the Workbench client: { "client_id": "posit-workbench", "client_secret": "CLIENT_SECRET", "scope": ["openid", "sas-compute.user_impersonation"], "authorized_grant_types": ["authorization_code", "refresh_token"], "redirect_uri": ["https://workbench.example.com/oauth_redirect_callback"], "access_token_validity": 36000, "refresh_token_validity": 86400, "autoapprove": ["openid", "sas-compute.user_impersonation"] } redirect_uri: for Workbench, https://workbench.example.com/oauth_redirect_callback. The path is fixed and does not contain the integration name. authorized_grant_types: authorization_code for the sign-in, and refresh_token so that Workbench can renew the access token. scope: openid and sas-compute.user_impersonation. autoapprove: skips the SAS Logon consent page for these scopes. access_token_validity and refresh_token_validity: lifetimes in seconds. Choose values that match your security policy. Register the Connect client the same way, with these differences: Use a different client_id, such as posit-connect. Set redirect_uri to https://connect.example.com/__oauth__/integrations/callback. If a proxy serves Connect under a path, include it, for example https://posit.example.com/connect/__oauth__/integrations/callback. For a Service Account integration, add client_credentials to authorized_grant_types. Connect Service Account integrations use the OAuth client credentials grant. warning A token from the client credentials grant identifies the OAuth client, not a person. Confirm with your SAS Viya administrator that SAS Compute accepts such a token, and which identity the Compute session runs as. SAS Compute might need a compute context that runs as a shared account.

documents.t: Add a section for SAS Viya to /etc/rstudio/oauth-clients.conf: [sas-viya] name=SAS Viya client-id=posit-workbench client-secret=CLIENT_SECRET authorize-url=https://viya.example.com/SASLogon/oauth/authorize token-url=https://viya.example.com/SASLogon/oauth/token scopes=openid,sas-compute.user_impersonation The scopes value is a comma-separated list. For several SAS Viya deployments, add one section for each, such as [sas-viya] and [sas-viya-test], each with its own SAS Logon client. The Positron SAS extension finds this integration by its token-url. Use the same SAS Viya host name in token-url as in the users' SAS Viya profiles. Restrict the file permissions, because it contains the client secret, and reload Workbench: sudo chmod 600 /etc/rstudio/oauth-clients.conf sudo chown rstudio-server:rstudio-server /etc/rstudio/oauth-clients.conf sudo rstudio-server reload
