documents.t: Create Custom OAuth integrations in Connect that point to SAS Logon. Most deployments create two integrations from the same SAS Logon client: SAS Viya (Viewer): each viewer signs in with their own SAS Viya identity. It works only with interactive content, such as Shiny apps. SAS Viya (Service Account): all viewers share one token. It works with interactive and rendered content, such as Quarto documents and scheduled reports. An administrator creates the integrations in the Connect dashboard or through the Connect Server API. The following request body creates the Viewer integration with a POST to /__api__/v1/oauth/integrations: { "name": "SAS Viya (Viewer)", "template": "custom", "config": { "auth_type": "Viewer", "auth_mode": "Confidential", "use_pkce": true, "authorization_uri": "https://viya.example.com/SASLogon/oauth/authorize", "token_uri": "https://viya.example.com/SASLogon/oauth/token", "client_id": "posit-connect", "client_secret": "CLIENT_SECRET", "scopes": "openid sas-compute.user_impersonation", "token_endpoint_auth_method": "client_secret_post" } } For the Service Account integration, set auth_type to Service Account and remove auth_mode and use_pkce. Those two options apply only to Viewer integrations. Publishers then add an integration to each content item. In the content settings, open the Runtime tab, and under Integrations, click Add Integrations. Rendered content offers only Service Account integrations.

On the Workbench homepage, click your user name, then Settings, then Managed Credentials. Under Custom OAuth, sign in to SAS Viya. Positron Pro and VS Code users can also sign in from the Available Credentials view. Click the information icon next to SAS Viya and copy the Integration ID. Store the ID in an environment variable, such as SAS_VIYA_INTEGRATION_ID in .Renviron or .env. The Managed Credentials page in Workbench. Under Custom OAuth, the SAS Viya integration is signed in, and its button signs the user out. Once you are signed in, new sessions receive the credential automatically. The New Session dialog lists it under Session Credentials, in Custom OAuth Credentials. The New Session dialog with the Custom OAuth Credentials section expanded, listing the SAS Viya integration. The integration ID stays the same between sessions. Code can also look it up by name with rstudioapi::findOAuthIntegration(name = "^SAS Viya$") in R, or Client().oauth.integrations.find_by(name="^SAS Viya$") in Python. Python with saspy​ saspy accepts a SAS Logon access token through its authtoken option. The viya definition in sascfg_personal.py needs only url and context: import os import saspy from posit.workbench import Client creds = Client().oauth.get_credentials(audience=os.environ["SAS_VIYA_INTEGRATION_ID"]) sas = saspy.SASsession(cfgname="viya", authtoken=creds["access_token"]) print(sas.submitLOG("proc options option=work; run;")) sas.endsas() get_credentials() returns None when the user has not signed in to the integration. R with sasquatch​ sas_connect() passes only cfgname to saspy, so the token must come from the saspy configuration. This sascfg_personal.py reads the token from a variable in the Python main module each time a session starts: import __main__ SAS_config_names = ['viya'] def __getattr__(name): # saspy looks up the definition by name for each SASsession if name == 'viya': return {'url': 'https://viya.example.com', 'context': 'SAS Studio compute context', 'authtoken': getattr(__main__, 'SAS_VIYA_TOKEN', None)} raise AttributeError(name) R code gets the token from Workbench and sets that variable on the Python main module through reticulate. py_set_attr() does this in one call. The shorter reticulate::py$SAS_VIYA_TOKEN <- ... fails in R, because R cannot assign to a name with a package prefix. library(sasquatch) creds <- rstudioapi::getOAuthCredentials( audience = Sys.getenv("SAS_VIYA_INTEGRATION_ID") ) reticulate::py_set_attr(reticulate::import_main(), "SAS_VIYA_TOKEN", creds$access_token) sas_connect(cfgname = "viya", reconnect = TRUE) sas_from_r(mtcars, "cars") sas_run_string("proc means data=cars; var mpg; run;") sas_disconnect() getOAuthCredentials() throws an error when the user has not signed in to the integration. The following screenshot shows the same steps in a Positron Pro session. It runs the plot.sas program from the demo repository on SAS Viya, with sas_run_string(). The Viewer pane shows the plot and the table that the program creates. An R console in Positron running sasquatch against SAS Viya. The code gets the token from Workbench, connects, and runs a SAS program. The Viewer pane shows the plot and the listing. Python code can use the same sascfg_personal.py. An authtoken argument to SASsession() takes precedence over the configuration. The SAS extension can export a SAS Viya profile as a saspy configuration (SAS: Export saspy Configuration). That configuration looks for a token each time saspy connects. In this order, it uses the SAS_VIYA_TOKEN environment variable, the SAS_VIYA_TOKEN variable on the Python main module (as above), the Workbench integration read with posit-sdk (when SAS_VIYA_INTEGRATION_ID or the profile's workbenchIntegration gives its ID), and the token file ~/.positron-sas/viya-token.json. The command SAS: Save Viya Token for saspy writes that file from the extension's own sign-in, readable only by the user, so that a Quarto render can use the same sign-in. Run it again when the token has expired. swat and sasctl​ swat accepts the token as the password argument when no username is given. sasctl accepts it as the token argument: import swat from sasctl import Session conn = swat.CAS("https://viya.example.com/cas-shared-default-http/", password=creds["access_token"]) print(conn.serverstatus()) with Session("viya.example.com", token=creds["access_token"]): ... # call sasctl services here

The token comes from Connect instead of Workbench. Connect never gives refresh tokens to content. Viewer integration Service Account integration Identity in SAS Viya Each viewer One shared identity Content types Interactive only, such as Shiny Interactive and rendered, such as Quarto and R Markdown Viewer sign-in Each viewer signs in to SAS Viya on first visit None R function connectapi::get_oauth_credentials() connectapi::get_oauth_content_credentials() Python function Client().oauth.get_credentials() Client().oauth.get_content_credentials() Use a Viewer integration when results depend on each viewer's SAS Viya permissions. Use a Service Account integration for rendered or scheduled content, and for content that all viewers may see with the same data. Shiny for R with a Viewer Integration​ The viewer's session token arrives in the Posit-Connect-User-Session-Token request header. Exchange it for the viewer's SAS Viya token: library(shiny) library(sasquatch) server <- function(input, output, session) { observeEvent(input$run_analysis, { user_token <- session$request$HTTP_POSIT_CONNECT_USER_SESSION_TOKEN creds <- connectapi::get_oauth_credentials(connectapi::connect(), user_token) reticulate::py_set_attr(reticulate::import_main(), "SAS_VIYA_TOKEN", creds$access_token) sas_connect(cfgname = "viya", reconnect = TRUE) # ... sas_from_r(), sas_run_string(), sas_to_r() ... sas_disconnect() }) } Shiny for Python with a Viewer Integration​ import saspy from posit.connect import Client from shiny import App, reactive, ui app_ui = ui.page_fluid(ui.input_action_button("run", "Run Analysis")) def server(input, output, session): @reactive.effect @reactive.event(input.run) def _(): user_token = session.http_conn.headers.get("Posit-Connect-User-Session-Token") creds = Client().oauth.get_credentials(user_token) sas = saspy.SASsession(cfgname="viya", authtoken=creds["access_token"]) # ... sas.df2sd(), sas.submit(), sas.sd2df() ... sas.endsas() app = App(app_ui, server) Quarto and R Markdown with a Service Account Integration​ Rendered content reads the content session token that Connect provides. This setup chunk works both in Workbench and on Connect: library(sasquatch) if (Sys.getenv("POSIT_PRODUCT") == "CONNECT") { creds <- connectapi::get_oauth_content_credentials(connectapi::connect()) } else { creds <- rstudioapi::getOAuthCredentials( audience = Sys.getenv("SAS_VIYA_INTEGRATION_ID") ) } reticulate::py_set_attr(reticulate::import_main(), "SAS_VIYA_TOKEN", creds$access_token) sas_connect(cfgname = "viya") In Python, Client().oauth.get_content_credentials() returns the token. If content has more than one integration, pass the integration ID as audience to choose one.

Workbench stores each user's OAuth tokens in its database, encrypted with the secure-cookie-key. Sessions call Workbench for a token with a cookie signed with the session-rpc-key. If Workbench creates new keys when it restarts, the stored tokens cannot be decrypted, and the integration shows "Custom OAuth integration 'sas-viya' has validation errors" until the user signs in again. Sessions that were running before the restart also cannot get tokens. Keep both keys, and the launcher keys, the same across restarts: On a server installation, the keys in /var/lib/rstudio-server and /etc/rstudio persist on disk. For several Workbench nodes, use the same secure-cookie-key on every node. In Kubernetes with the rstudio-workbench Helm chart (checked with chart version 0.10.3), store the keys in one Kubernetes secret, with the keys launcher.pem, launcher.pub, secure-cookie-key, and session-rpc-key. Reference it with secureCookieKey.existingSecret and launcherPem.existingSecret. Add launcher.pub and session-rpc-key with config.existingSecrets. The chart's secureCookieKey.value and launcherPem.value settings do not mount the keys into the pod, so Workbench creates new ones on every start. The secure-cookie-key must be at least 32 characters long, for example from openssl rand -hex 32. Workbench does not start with a shorter key.

saspy uses the token for every call to the Compute service and does not renew a token that it did not request. Connect again with a fresh token when the token expires. sasquatch keeps one SAS session for each R process. With a Viewer integration, set Max connections per process to 1 for the Shiny app, so that viewers do not share a SAS session. Viewer integrations do not work with rendered content, anonymous public access, or share links. In Workbench Jobs, token retrieval stops working 7 days after the job is submitted. Custom OAuth credentials are not available in JupyterLab sessions. The access token's scopes limit what the code can do in SAS Viya. Confirm that the scopes you register permit CAS and SAS Viya web service calls before you rely on swat or sasctl.

Positron runs SAS next to R and Python. With the SAS extension, SAS gets its own console and the same Viewer, Plots pane, Connections pane, and Data Explorer as the other languages, and Posit Assistant can work with SAS code and results. For the full list, see Positron SAS Extension Features. SAS can run in the session itself or on a separate SAS server. The editor experience is the same. The difference is where SAS runs and how the extension connects to it. The connection types are the ones described in Profile Definitions and Connection Types. Variant Where SAS runs Connection Status SAS installed with Workbench In the session, from a SAS installation on the Workbench host or in the session image Local (stdio), profile added automatically for common paths Supported Remote SAS over SSH On a SAS 9.4 or SAS Analytics Pro server SSH, profile written by the user Supported Remote SAS Viya On SAS Viya compute REST, profile written by the user, sign-in through Workbench Supported

No SAS server available: run SAS in the session, from a SAS installation that the administrator adds like R and Python. An existing SAS 9.4 or SAS Analytics Pro server: connect over SSH. Code and data stay on that server. SAS Viya: connect over REST, with the same Workbench sign-in to SAS Viya as code in sessions. This variant also gives access to SAS Content, SAS server files, and the Clinical Repository.

An administrator installs SAS where Workbench sessions run, in the same way as R and Python: on the Workbench host for local sessions, or in the session image for container sessions. Positron then runs SAS in the session through the local (stdio) connection.

documents.t: SAS in the Positron console, with all the Positron SAS extension features that work with local SAS SAS in the terminal, by its installation path No SAS server and no network connection to SAS: code and data stay in the session

Any Workbench release with Positron sessions The Positron SAS extension 0.4.0 or later. Automatic profiles for SAS 9.4 need version 0.5.0 or later. SAS installed and licensed on the Workbench host or in the session image. The license is applied at installation, as for any SAS installation, so Workbench does not provide it.
Install SAS on the Workbench host, or add it to the session image, and apply the SAS license. Make sure that users can run the SAS launcher and write to the SAS WORK location.

The extension adds a local connection profile automatically when it finds SAS. It uses the first executable launcher in this order: The paths in the SAS.localSasPaths setting /opt/sas/viya/home/SASFoundation/sas, the path in SAS Analytics Pro and SAS Viya-based installations Common SAS 9.4 locations, such as /opt/sas/SASHome/SASFoundation/9.4/bin/sas_u8 and /usr/local/SASHome/SASFoundation/9.4/bin/sas_u8 sas on the PATH For SAS 9.4, the extension uses the UTF-8 launcher bin/sas_u8, because it reads SAS output as UTF-8. SAS.localSasPaths is a machine setting, so an administrator can set it for all users of a Workbench host or session image when SAS is installed elsewhere. The extension adds the profile once: a deleted profile stays deleted, and an existing stdio profile prevents it. Users can also add the profile to their Positron settings themselves: "SAS.connectionProfiles": { "activeProfile": "local", "profiles": { "local": { "connectionType": "stdio", "saspath": "/opt/sas/SASHome/SASFoundation/9.4/bin/sas_u8" } } } Then choose SAS (local) in the interpreter picker, or open a .sas file to start the SAS console. For all profile settings, see the stdio connection profile. The Start New Console Session picker in Positron, listing SAS (local) next to the Python interpreters. The SAS console runs your code. Positron shows the rendered output in the Viewer pane. A SAS console in Positron after running PROC SGPLOT and PROC PRINT on sashelp.class. The log and listing appear in the console. The scatter plot and the formatted table appear in the Viewer pane.

Every session that runs SAS uses the session's CPUs and memory, so size sessions for SAS workloads. The SAS license terms apply to every machine and container that runs SAS. The console cannot interrupt a running submission. It stays busy until the code finishes, and a message offers to restart the session, which stops SAS.
Positron connects to a SAS 9.4 server, or to a standalone SAS Analytics Pro server, over SSH. SAS runs on that server, and the session sends code and receives the log and results.

Make sure that sessions can reach the SAS host on its SSH port. Each user creates an SSH key in their home directory, for example ~/.ssh/id_ed25519, and adds the public key to their account on the SAS host.

Add a profile to the Positron settings: "SAS.connectionProfiles": { "activeProfile": "sas-server", "profiles": { "sas-server": { "connectionType": "ssh", "host": "sas.example.com", "port": 22, "username": "jdoe", "saspath": "/opt/sas/SASHome/SASFoundation/9.4/sas", "privateKeyFilePath": "/home/jdoe/.ssh/id_ed25519" } } } For SAS Analytics Pro, saspath is /opt/sas/viya/home/SASFoundation/sas. One of these ways to sign in: Through Workbench (recommended): a custom OAuth integration for SAS Viya in Workbench, set up as in Configure the Workbench User OAuth Provider, and Positron Pro sessions With SAS Logon in the browser: an OAuth client in SAS Logon for the extension's sign-in. SAS Viya 4 2022.11 and later have one for SAS's extension, so clientId can stay empty. Check that it allows the Positron SAS extension's sign-in in your environment.

For sign-in through Workbench, add the SAS Viya section to oauth-clients.conf as described in Configure the Workbench User OAuth Provider. For sign-in with SAS Logon, also give them the client ID, if your SAS Viya needs one. For the client and profile settings, see the SAS Viya connection profile.

For sign-in through Workbench, sign in to the SAS Viya integration once: on the Workbench homepage, click your user name, then Settings, then Managed Credentials, and sign in under Custom OAuth. Positron Pro users can also sign in from the Available Credentials view. Add a profile to the Positron settings: "SAS.connectionProfiles": { "activeProfile": "viya", "profiles": { "viya": { "connectionType": "rest", "endpoint": "https://viya.example.com" } } } Choose SAS (viya) in the interpreter picker. The console shows the SAS log of a PROC SGPLOT and PROC PRINT run, and the Viewer pane shows the scatter plot and the table. With the default "authentication": "auto", the extension uses the Workbench integration when one matches the profile's endpoint. If you have not signed in to it yet, a message asks you to sign in in Workbench, or to sign in with SAS Logon instead. Without a matching integration, or outside Workbench, the extension opens SAS Logon in the browser. Two profile settings change this: authentication: "workbench" always uses the Workbench integration and fails with an explanation if there is none. "sasLogon" always signs in with SAS Logon. workbenchIntegration: the ID of the integration to use, when several integrations point to the same SAS Viya. The ID is shown under the information icon next to the integration in Managed Credentials. The extension keeps the Workbench token in memory and gets a new one from Workbench before it expires. Signing out in the Positron Accounts menu stops the extension from using the token. It does not sign you out of the integration in Workbench.

Sign-in through Workbench needs a Positron Pro session, which can reach Workbench. In Positron outside Workbench, the extension signs in with SAS Logon. Consoles that connect to different SAS Viya servers at the same time are not supported. Consoles against the same SAS Viya server each get their own compute session. Workbench must keep its keys across restarts, as described in Keep Tokens across Workbench Restarts.
These topics apply to every scenario. The examples come from a reference deployment, which runs Posit Workbench, Posit Connect, and SAS Viya in one Amazon EKS cluster.

SAS and Posit work best when a person has the same identity on both. Single sign-on: Workbench and Connect sign users in through the same identity provider as SAS Viya. In the reference deployment, both use Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) clients in the SAS Viya Keycloak realm. The same user account: a shared LDAP directory gives each user the same user name, user ID, and group ID in Workbench sessions and in SAS Viya compute. The directory is federated into Keycloak and read by Workbench through SSSD. Shared home directories: Workbench and SAS Viya compute mount the same /home file system. Files created in a Workbench session are available to SAS Viya code under the same path and owner, and the other way around. With these in place, users sign in once in the browser, and files move between SAS and R or Python without copying.

Posit Assistant in Positron works with SAS through the SAS extension: it lists libraries and tables, reads SAS output and graphs, writes Quarto reports with {sas} chunks, and can create a saspy configuration and save your SAS Viya token for it. See Positron SAS Extension Features. The Assistant needs access to a language model. In the reference deployment, Workbench sessions use Amazon Bedrock through AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles for service accounts.

The extension records who ran which SAS code: An optional audit log in JSON Lines format for every submission A comment with the user and session on every submitted program Macro variables with the Positron and Workbench session, for use in SAS code and logs Tags on SAS Viya compute sessions and jobs with the Workbench user and session See Traceability for the settings.

Positron opens SAS data sets (.sas7bdat) and transport files (.xpt) in the Data Explorer through the active SAS session. For a file in the session, the SAS session assigns a library to the file's folder, so the SAS session must be able to read that folder. That is always the case with local SAS, and with remote SAS when it shares the file system with Workbench, as SAS Viya does in the reference deployment. Files from the Clinical Repository or SAS Content are copied into WORK first. R and Python code can read the same files with packages such as haven and pyreadstat.

documents.t: Large visualizations generated from Python notebook cells can produce extremely large SVG output. In some cases, this can lead to notebook rendering issues, slow performance, or errors such as: Error: Cannot create a string longer than 0x1fffffe8 characters Solution As a workaround, generate the graph in a lighter-weight format, such as PNG, instead of using the default SVG output format. If you are using SAS.show(): SAS.show(fig, filetype="png") If you are using SAS.pyplot(): SAS.pyplot(fig, filetype="png") Example Instead of: SAS.show(fig) use: SAS.show(fig, filetype="png") Using PNG output can significantly reduce the size of the generated graph output and help avoid notebook rendering and performance issues when working with large matplotlib or seaborn visualizations.

documents.t: You need to manually trust your server's certificate using the steps below: Get your server's certificate file 1.1. Access your SAS Viya endpoint with Google Chrome or Microsoft Edge 1.2. Click the "lock" icon on the left of the URL on the address bar. The site information panel opens. 1.3. Click "Connection is secure", then click "Certificate is valid". The Certificate Viewer opens. 1.4. Click the "Details" tab, then click "Export". Select "Base64-encoded ASCII, certificate chain" and save it to a file. For Mac OS, you can install the certificate file into your Keychain Access and trust the certificate. If you are using another operating system or you don't want to add the certificate to your system, open VS Code Settings > SAS: User Provided Certificates. Enter the full path of the certificate file. Restart VS Code. If the steps above do not work, you can bypass the certificate check: Set the environment variable NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED to 0 to bypass the certificate check. Shut down all VS Code instances and then restart the application with the updated environment variable. If you are connecting to a remote workspace, set the environment variable on the remote system and terminate all VS Code server processes (for example, run ps -aux | grep vscode-server on the remote Linux machine to see the processes).

documents.t: Each release of the SAS Extension for Positron is published as a VSIX file in the Releases of the posit-dev/positron-sas-extension repository. For now, you install the extension from that file. Open the latest release and download the VSIX file from Assets. The file is named positron-sas-<version>.vsix, for example positron-sas-0.5.0.vsix. In Positron, open the Extensions view by clicking the Extensions icon in the Activity Bar. Click the ... (Views and More Actions) menu at the top of the Extensions view, and choose Install from VSIX.... You can also open the command palette (F1, or Ctrl+Shift+P on Windows or Linux, or Shift+CMD+P on macOS) and run Extensions: Install from VSIX.... Select the downloaded file. When the installation is complete, reload the window if Positron asks you to. To update the extension, install the VSIX file of the newer release in the same way. After the installation, create a connection profile as described in Configuring the SAS Extension. If SAS is installed on the same machine, the extension adds a local profile for it automatically. See Local SAS.

documents.t: In a Positron Pro session in Posit Workbench, you install the extension the same way. The extension is installed in your home directory, so it stays available in your later sessions, and the installation can take a few minutes. If sessions have no access to GitHub, download the VSIX file on another machine and upload it to your home directory in the session, then choose Install from VSIX... and select it. For the ways to run SAS in Workbench, see SAS with Posit Workbench.

The repository builds the extension after every change that reaches the main branch, and publishes each build as a pre-release. Use a development build to try a change before the next release. A development build can contain unfinished changes. Open the Releases page and find the newest entry marked Pre-release. Its name is Positron SAS <version>-dev.<number>, where <version> is the last release. Download the VSIX file from Assets, and install it as described above. The notes of a pre-release list the unreleased changes and the commits since the last release. The VSIX file keeps the version number of the last release, so Positron shows the same version for a development build and for the release before it. To return to a released version, install the VSIX file of the latest release. The repository keeps the five newest development builds.

The SAS Extension for Positron builds on the SAS Extension for Visual Studio Code, whose documentation is in the other sections of this site. To use SAS's own extension in Visual Studio Code, install the latest version of Visual Studio Code (version 1.89 or later), and then: Open the Extensions view by clicking the Extensions icon in the Activity Bar on the left side of the Visual Studio Code window. Search for the 'Official' SAS extension, and click the Install button. Once the installation is complete, the Install button changes to the Manage button. NOTE: For macOS users, some environments may require additional certificate installation steps before connecting successfully to a SAS Viya server. Please refer to the FAQ (see "Why did I get the Unable to parse decrypted password error?") for details.
